analysis.one_liner: Exempts certain large nonbank financial firms from annual Dodd-Frank stress tests.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in 2019 and died without ever getting a vote or a hearing-level action beyond subcommittee referral.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2008 financial crisis, the Dodd-Frank law required large financial companies to run stress tests — periodic checks of whether they could survive a severe economic downturn. This bill would change that rule so that only companies overseen by federal banking regulators or the housing-finance regulator must run them. Companies whose main regulator is the Securities and Exchange Commission or the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — such as broker-dealers and swap dealers — would no longer be required to test their own ability to weather a crisis, though those agencies could still order such tests by regulation. The bill never advanced past its first committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Large financial companies that are not banks and whose primary regulator is the SEC or CFTC, such as broker-dealers and swap dealers, would gain by avoiding the recurring cost and public scrutiny of mandatory stress tests under Dodd-Frank's section 165(i).

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends Dodd-Frank section 165(i)(2) so the stress-test mandate applies only to companies whose primary financial regulatory agency is a federal banking agency or the Federal Housing Finance Agency, releasing SEC- and CFTC-regulated companies from the automatic requirement.

It directs the SEC and CFTC to drop out of the group of regulators that must conduct stress tests on the firms they supervise, while giving each agency discretionary authority to issue regulations requiring periodic financial-condition analyses, including available liquidity, under adverse economic conditions.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the risk if large nonbank firms are less regularly examined for their ability to survive a downturn; when such firms fail in a crisis, the fallout lands on markets, retirement accounts, and historically on taxpayer-supported rescues.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ordinary people exposed to nonbank failures

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection: Dodd-Frank stress tests were adopted after the 2008 crisis, when the failure of large nonbank firms such as AIG and Lehman spread losses across the economy; exempting SEC- and CFTC-regulated firms from the automatic requirement removes a recurring check on whether they could survive a severe downturn.

Supporters of the rollback would acknowledge the trade-off: stress tests impose real compliance costs on regulated firms, and the bill leaves those costs only on bank-regulated companies rather than spreading the burden.

The bill gives the SEC and CFTC discretionary power to require financial-condition analyses, so protection for the public depends on those agencies choosing to act; the automatic mandate is what disappears.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to firms is a lower, lighter regulatory burden; the cost is that fewer large financial companies would be automatically tested for crisis resilience. Because nonbank failures in 2008 damaged the wider economy, the trade-off weighs mainly toward concentrated industry benefit with diffuse public risk. The bill is narrow — it does not repeal bank stress tests — but its effect runs one way.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services and Agriculture Committees, then sent to a Financial Services subcommittee, and it never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Barry Loudermilk (R-GA) introduced the bill on July 25, 2019, joined by Rep. Ed Perlmutter (D-CO) as its one cosponsor.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services and, in addition, to the House Committee on Agriculture.
On August 29, 2019, it was referred to the Financial Services Subcommittee on Commodity Exchanges, Energy, and Credit.
No further action appears in the record: the bill never reached a committee vote or the House floor, and it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large nonbank financial firms that would have faced the exempted stress tests are better off, since the rollback never needed to be fought — the bill simply stalled in committee, and the existing Dodd-Frank stress-test requirement remained in force.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nonbank financial firms spared the rule change

for.name: Rep. Barry Loudermilk
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt SEC- and CFTC-regulated nonbank companies from Dodd-Frank stress tests.

for.name: Rep. Ed Perlmutter
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only member from either party to sign on.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of primary jurisdiction (chaired by Rep. Maxine Waters, D-CA); Chair never advanced the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Commodity Exchanges, Energy, and Credit and never brought it to a committee vote, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor, and no votes were ever taken, so its partisan support was never tested.

industries.industry: Nonbank financial companies (SEC- and CFTC-regulated firms such as broker-dealers and swap dealers)
industries.note: The bill would lift the automatic Dodd-Frank requirement that these firms run stress tests of their ability to survive adverse economic conditions, leaving only optional agency rules in its place. Their gain is reduced compliance cost and less recurring examination; the offsetting risk — firms failing a downturn with less scrutiny — falls on markets and ordinary investors.
Banks and their federal banking regulators would remain fully subject to the stress-test regime, so the bill creates no change for them; they are only relatively more scrutinized than nonbank peers.
